title: Staffing
summary: Staffing is the managerial function of filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure with the right people. This chapter covers the importance of staffing, staffing as a part of human resource management, the staffing process, sources of recruitment, the selection process, and training and development with their methods.

notes.heading: Meaning and Importance of Staffing
notes.html:
Staffing means putting people to jobs: right person at the right job at the right time. It includes estimating manpower requirements, recruitment, selection, placement, training, appraisal, promotion and compensation.

Importance:

  1. Obtains competent personnel – helps discover and obtain the right people for various jobs.
  2. Higher performance – putting the right person on the right job improves performance.
  3. Continuous survival and growth – ensures a steady supply of capable people through succession planning.
  4. Optimum utilisation of human resources – avoids over-manning and under-manning.
  5. Improves job satisfaction and morale – through fair rewards, training and career growth.

notes.heading: Staffing as a Part of Human Resource Management
notes.html:
Human Resource Management (HRM) is a wider concept that includes staffing and many specialised activities, handled by the HR department.

  • Recruitment, selection and placement
  • Analysing jobs and preparing job descriptions
  • Developing compensation and incentive plans
  • Training and development of employees
  • Maintaining labour relations and union–management relations
  • Handling grievances and complaints
  • Social security and welfare schemes
  • Defending the company in lawsuits on labour matters

Evolution: labour welfare officer → personnel management → HRM (treating employees as valuable resources).

Staffing is both a function of every manager (each manager selects and trains his team) and a separate department (HR department) in large firms.

notes.heading: Staffing Process
notes.html:
1. Estimating manpower requirements – workload analysis (number and type of people needed) and workforce analysis (number and type available); the gap shows over- or under-staffing. Job description and job specification are prepared.
  2. Recruitment – searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply.
  3. Selection – choosing the best candidates from the pool of applicants.
  4. Placement and orientation – placement puts the selected employee on the job; orientation (induction) introduces him to the organisation, colleagues and rules.
  5. Training and development – improving skills and preparing employees for growth.
  6. Performance appraisal – evaluating actual performance against standards.
  7. Promotion and career planning – placing employees in higher positions with more responsibility and pay.
  8. Compensation – direct financial payments (wages, salary, incentives) and indirect payments (insurance, holidays).

Memory aid: E-R-S-P-T-P-P-C – Every Recruiter Selects People To Promote Productive Colleagues.

notes.heading: Recruitment: Internal Sources
notes.html:
Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. It is a positive process.

Internal sources:

  • Transfer – shifting an employee from one job to another of similar nature, status and pay.
  • Promotion – shifting an employee to a higher position with more responsibility, status and pay.

Merits: motivates employees; simplifies selection and placement (employees already known); transfers help balance workforce; filling posts is cheaper; less time and cost on training.

Limitations: no fresh talent (scope for induction of new ideas is limited); employees may become lethargic if promotion is assured; spirit of competition reduced; frequent transfers reduce productivity; not possible for a new firm.

notes.heading: Recruitment: External Sources
notes.html:
• Direct recruitment – notice on the notice board for casual vacancies; candidates assemble at the gate.
  • Casual callers – applications already received from job seekers kept in a database.
  • Advertisement – in newspapers, journals and online, for a wider choice.
  • Employment exchanges – government-run offices matching job seekers with vacancies (mainly unskilled and semi-skilled jobs).
  • Placement agencies and management consultants – provide a database of candidates, especially for professional and technical posts.
  • Campus recruitment – recruitment from colleges and institutes for fresh talent.
  • Recommendations of employees – existing employees recommend friends and relatives.
  • Labour contractors – supply unskilled workers on short notice.
  • Web publishing / job portals – websites like job portals are used by both employers and job seekers.

Merits: qualified personnel; wider choice; fresh talent; competitive spirit among existing staff.

Limitations: dissatisfaction among existing staff; lengthy process; costly.

notes.heading: Selection Process
notes.html:
Selection is choosing the most suitable candidate from those who applied. It is a negative process because many applicants are rejected.

  1. Preliminary screening – eliminates unqualified or unfit applicants based on application forms and preliminary interviews.
  2. Selection tests – intelligence tests (IQ, ability to make decisions), aptitude tests (potential to learn new skills), personality tests (emotions, maturity, value system), trade tests (existing skills and knowledge), interest tests (pattern of interests).
  3. Employment interview – formal, in-depth conversation to evaluate suitability.
  4. Reference and background checks – verification from references, previous employers and police records.
  5. Selection decision – final decision taken from among those who passed the tests, interview and checks, usually by the concerned manager.
  6. Medical examination – to ensure physical fitness.
  7. Job offer – offer (appointment) letter stating the date of joining.
  8. Contract of employment – document stating terms and conditions: job title, duties, pay, hours, leave, termination conditions.
BasisRecruitmentSelection
MeaningSearching and attracting candidatesChoosing the best among candidates
NaturePositive processNegative process
SequencePrecedes selectionFollows recruitment
ObjectiveCreate a large pool of applicantsPick the most suitable candidate
ContractNo contract createdLeads to a contract of employment

notes.heading: Training and Development: Concepts and Importance
notes.html:
BasisTrainingEducationDevelopment
MeaningIncreasing knowledge and skills for a specific jobIncreasing general knowledge and understandingOverall growth of the employee
FocusJob-orientedBroad, conceptualCareer-oriented
ScopeNarrowWideWide
Used forOperativesEveryoneManagers / executives

Benefits to the organisation: systematic learning reduces wastage; higher productivity and quality; equips future managers; increases morale and reduces absenteeism and turnover; quick response to technological change.

Benefits to employees: better career opportunities; higher earnings; more efficient use of machines, so fewer accidents; greater satisfaction and morale.

notes.heading: Methods of Training
notes.html:
On-the-job methods (learning while doing, at the workplace):

  • Apprenticeship training – trainee works under a master worker for a prescribed period, mainly for trades like plumbing and electrical work.
  • Coaching – superior guides and instructs the trainee as a coach.
  • Internship training – joint programme of educational institutes and business firms; students get practical exposure.
  • Job rotation – shifting the trainee from one department to another to broaden understanding.

Off-the-job methods (learning away from the workplace):

  • Vestibule training – a dummy model of the actual work set-up is created away from the workplace; used when expensive or sophisticated equipment is involved (e.g. pilots on simulators).
  • Classroom lectures, films, case studies, computer modelling and programmed instruction.
BasisOn-the-jobOff-the-job
PlaceAt the workplaceAway from the workplace
ApproachLearning by doingLearning before doing
CostLess costlyMore costly
ProductionProduction goes onNo production during training
ExpertSuperior or experienced workerSpecialists or experts

mcqs.q: Ankit, a sales executive, was shifted from the Delhi branch to the Jaipur branch on the same post and salary. Which source of recruitment is this?
mcqs.explanation: Shifting to a similar job with the same status and pay is a transfer, an internal source.

mcqs.q: Which test is used to measure a candidate's potential to learn new skills?
mcqs.explanation: An aptitude test measures the capacity to develop new skills.

mcqs.q: Recruitment is called a positive process because:
options: It attracts as many candidates as possible to apply
mcqs.explanation: Recruitment stimulates people to apply, creating a large pool; selection, which rejects candidates, is negative.

mcqs.q: An airline trains its pilots on flight simulators before they fly real aircraft. Which method of training is this?
mcqs.explanation: Training on dummy equipment away from the actual workplace is vestibule training.

mcqs.q: In the staffing process, which step immediately follows selection?
mcqs.explanation: After selection, the employee is placed on the job and introduced to the organisation: placement and orientation.

mcqs.q: A firm found that it needs 50 machine operators but has only 38. Which part of estimating manpower requirements revealed the shortfall?
mcqs.explanation: Comparing required (workload) and available (workforce) manpower shows under-staffing.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a limitation of internal sources of recruitment?
options: It limits the entry of fresh talent
mcqs.explanation: Filling vacancies from within reduces the scope for fresh talent and new ideas.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Selection is a negative process.
Reason (R): In selection, a large number of applicants are rejected and only a few are chosen.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Selection is negative precisely because it involves rejection of most candidates.

mcqs.q: Commerce students of a college worked at a CA firm for two months as part of their course. This is:
mcqs.explanation: A joint programme of an educational institution and a firm is internship training.

mcqs.q: A trainee electrician works under the guidance of a master electrician for three years. This is:
mcqs.explanation: Learning a trade under a master worker for a fixed period is apprenticeship training.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Training is job-oriented.
Reason (R): Development aims at the overall growth of an employee.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Both statements are true, but R describes development and does not explain why training is job-oriented.

mcqs.q: A factory needing 20 unskilled workers urgently for a week put up a notice at its gate. Which source is used?
mcqs.explanation: Putting a notice at the gate for casual vacancies is direct recruitment.

questions.answerHtml: Orientation (induction) is introducing the selected employee to other employees, the organisation and its rules and policies so that he becomes familiar with the work environment.

  3. Optimum utilisation of human resources – it prevents both over-manning and under-manning.

questions.q: State any four merits of external sources of recruitment.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Qualified personnel – the firm can attract qualified and trained people.
  2. Wider choice – a large number of applicants are available to choose from.
  3. Fresh talent – new people bring fresh ideas and skills.
  4. Competitive spirit – existing staff work harder to compete with outsiders.

questions.q: Explain the steps in the process of selection.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Preliminary screening – applications are scrutinised and unqualified applicants are eliminated.
  2. Selection tests – intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade and interest tests are conducted to measure suitability.
  3. Employment interview – an in-depth conversation to assess the candidate and give him information about the job.
  4. Reference and background checks – information given by the candidate is verified from references and previous employers.
  5. Selection decision – the final decision is made from among candidates who cleared the earlier stages, usually by the concerned manager.
  6. Medical examination – ensures the candidate is physically fit.
  7. Job offer – an appointment letter is issued with the date of joining.
  8. Contract of employment – a written contract states terms such as job title, duties, salary, working hours and termination conditions.

questions.q: Healthy Bites Ltd. needs 10 new delivery executives and a finance manager. The HR manager first calculated how many people were needed. For delivery executives, he asked existing staff to recommend friends; for the finance manager, he advertised on a job portal. After tests and interviews, the selected people were introduced to the company's culture and colleagues. Identify and explain the steps of staffing mentioned.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Estimating manpower requirements – 'calculated how many people were needed'. Workload and workforce analysis is done to find the number and type of employees required.
  2. Recruitment – 'asked existing staff to recommend friends … advertised on a job portal'. Searching for prospective employees and encouraging them to apply, using external sources (recommendations of employees, web publishing).
  3. Selection – 'after tests and interviews'. Choosing the most suitable candidates from among the applicants.
  4. Placement and orientation – 'introduced to the company's culture and colleagues'. The employee is placed on the job and familiarised with the organisation.
